| [NOTE-267](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-267.md) | Personal Autonomy | The entry sorts accounts of self-government into four families: "coherentist" (hierarchical desires, Frankfurt; evaluative judgments, Watson; plans, Bratman; caring; character), reasons-responsive, responsiveness-to-reasoning (Christman, Mele) and incompatibilist, with relational conditions as a compatible add-on. | [NOTE-270](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-270.md) | Compatibilism | The entry sorts compatibilism by which incompatibilist premise it denies: that free will requires the ability to do otherwise, that determinism precludes it, or that free will requires ultimate sourcehood. | [NOTE-374](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-374.md) | Personal Identity | A survey of the persistence debate with an animalist's emphasis. It separates seven questions, argues that the persistence question concerns numerical identity and must not presuppose person essentialism, and sets out psychological-continuity, brute-physical and anticriterialist answers. Fission and the too-many-thinkers objection are the two arguments that do the work. It avoids the word "self". One in-text citation (Olson and Witt 2020) has no matching bibliography entry. | Read |
| [NOTE-378](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-378.md) | Personal Identity | Wiggins's division case shows that what matters in survival need not be one-one, so it is not identity; fusion and imagined beings that divide show it comes in degrees. Q-memory and q-intention describe the relations without presupposing identity. Continuity (transitive) is distinguished from connectedness (degree), and successive selves are proposed in place of one underlying person. The principle of self-interest then has no independent force. §I is argued; the priority of connectedness is asserted; §VI is a sketch. | Read |
| [NOTE-382](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-382.md) | Shanahan — Simulacra as Conscious Exotica | A Wittgensteinian treatment: consciousness talk is anchored in what is public, so an exotic entity is a candidate only if we could engineer an encounter with it in a shared world. Disembodied chat agents are not candidates; virtually embodied ones could be. On the self: no "self worth preserving" without body, history and autobiographical memory, and no "person behind the mask" for a role player, whose identity is a shifting distribution of roles. Argued by method and scenario; nothing is measured. | Read |
| [NOTE-383](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-383.md) | Against Narrativity | Rejects the descriptive and the normative Narrativity theses. Separates Diachronic from Episodic self-experience, and form-finding, story-telling and revision within Narrativity. Places Dennett, Schechtman, Sartre and himself on that grid. Argues that Episodic lives are normal and can be good, that a from-the-inside memory need not present as one's own, and that self-narration risks falsification. The argument is testimony and distinction-drawing; the empirical claims are asserted. | Read |
| [NOTE-385](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-385.md) | Of Identity and Diversity | Identity is relative to the idea the name stands for: same mass, same life (oak, horse, man), same consciousness (person). A person is a thinking being that "can consider itself as itself", and personal identity reaches as far back as consciousness can be extended, independent of substance. Man and person come apart (prince and cobbler; day-man and night-man), and "person" is "a forensic term" grounding reward and punishment. Argued from cases and intuitions; "the same consciousness" is never defined. | Read |
| [NOTE-394](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-394.md) | Haslanger — Gender and Race: (What) Are They? | An explicitly ameliorative ("analytical") account. Gender and race are defined as hierarchical social positions: a woman is someone regularly observed or imagined to have bodily features presumed to indicate a female's reproductive role, marked by that within the dominant ideology for subordinate positions, and subordinated in part because of it. Racialized groups are defined in parallel from features presumed to show ancestral links to a region. Gender in general and ethnicity are the non-hierarchical genus. The commonality and normativity objections are met by appeal to the project's values. Stipulative, with no evidence. | Read |
| [NOTE-465](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-465.md) | The Sources of Normativity | Korsgaard's Tanner Lectures. The normative question (what justifies morality's claims on us) is not answered by voluntarism, substantive realism or reflective endorsement alone. Reflective consciousness forces us to act on reasons, and so to identify with a law: a "practical identity", the description under which we value ourselves. Obligation is the reflective rejection of a threat to that identity. Valuing any identity commits us to valuing humanity, reasons are public, and animals' pain can obligate us. Argued, but "sketchy" by its own account. | Read |
| [NOTE-545](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-545.md) | Freedom of the Will and the Concept of a Person | Persons differ from other creatures in the structure of the will: they have second-order volitions, desires that a given desire be the one that moves them to act, and wantons do not. Forming one is identifying with a desire. Freedom of the will is having the will one wants, and a decisive identification ends the series of higher orders "without cutting it off arbitrarily" (p. 16). Responsibility needs neither a free will nor alternatives: the willing addict acts of his own free will. The view is neutral on determinism, and on how the will came to be (n. 10). | Read |
| [NOTE-546](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-546.md) | Alternate Possibilities and Moral Responsibility | Frankfurt argues that PAP is false because circumstances can make an action unavoidable without bringing it about: Black stands ready to make Jones4 act and never needs to, so Jones4 is as responsible, for blame or praise, as he would be without Black (§IV). A fact that explains nothing about the action cannot excuse it (§V). The replacement principle excuses only an agent who acted "only because he could not have done otherwise", and Frankfurt says it is compatible with determinism. | Read |
| [NOTE-547](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-547.md) | Stories and the Meaning of Life | Fischer's own sketch of his framework (guidance control, not regulative control, is the freedom-relevant condition; guidance control is ownership plus moderate reasons-responsiveness; responsibility is historical and compatible with determinism; the Frankfurt cases' moral is the actual sequence), followed by the paper's thesis: acting freely is artistic self-expression that gives a life narrative value, a product judged mainly morally and prudentially, so the activity's aesthetic nature does not fix how the life is evaluated. | Read |
| [NOTE-548](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-548.md) | Moral Responsibility | A survey of moral responsibility. Its most exact reports, for this record: Fischer and Ravizza's guidance control as an owned, moderately reasons-responsive mechanism, with page references (§2.3); Wolf's critique of Real Self views and the requirement that an agent be able to form her values on the basis of the True and the Good (§3.1.1); and the moral competence condition, through JoJo (§3.2). Wolf's praise/blame asymmetry is noted in one sentence. | Read |
| [NOTE-575](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-575.md) | Précis of Responsibility and Control: A Theory of Moral Responsibility | The authors' own summary of Responsibility and Control. Moral responsibility requires guidance control, the agent's ownership of the mechanism that actually issues in action plus that mechanism's moderate reasons-responsiveness. Ownership comes from taking responsibility, a historical matter of dispositional self-beliefs acquired in appropriate ways. The result is compatible with causal determinism. | Read |
| [NOTE-579](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-579.md) | Responsiveness and Moral Responsibility | Fischer's first statement of reasons-responsiveness. Frankfurt-type cases show an agent can be responsible though he could not have done otherwise, so what must respond to reasons is the mechanism that actually issues in the action, not the agent. Weak responsiveness suffices: the actual kind of mechanism would do otherwise in some world with sufficient reason to. The result is semicompatibilism. | Read |
| [NOTE-698](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-698.md) | Floridi — Distributed morality in an information society | Distributed morality (DM) is the case where morally loaded actions of a multiagent system result from interactions among its members that are each morally neutral or negligible. The model is distributed knowledge: A knows P∨Q, B knows ¬P, and only the "supra-agent" AB knows Q. The paper models neutrality with two moral thresholds, which make environments fault-tolerant to small evils and inert to small goods, and it names the task of aggregating potential goods and fragmenting potential evils. It introduces "infraethics", the first-order framework of moral enablers (trust, privacy, transparency …) that is not morally good in itself. The analogy is not exact. Distributed knowledge combines different contents logically, while every example of DM sums contributions of one kind past a threshold, so what separates DM from a sum of actions is the threshold on moral evaluation, a parameter the paper leaves unspecified. No criterion of agency is applied to the supra-agent, and responsibility for DM, which Floridi & Sanders 2004 promised, is still not given. | Read |
| [NOTE-699](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-699.md) | Floridi — Faultless responsibility | When a morally loaded outcome C emerges from morally neutral interactions in a network of agents, nobody intends C, so an ethics that makes intention necessary assigns no responsibility for it. Floridi proposes to allocate it anyway: identify C and the network causally accountable for it, then make every node "prima facie equally and maximally responsible" (p. 7), overridable by showing no involvement, with the rule made common knowledge so that agents restrain one another. Back propagation, strict liability and common knowledge are borrowed as inspiration, and the paper says so. Two Dutch Supreme Court cases illustrate it. The argument is by design, not derivation. "Responsibility" here is causal accountability turned into a forward-looking corrective signal, which is what Floridi & Sanders 2004 called accountability and kept apart from responsibility. The paper never addresses that distinction, and in one of its own two examples the default is overridden by ease of rectification, which is a control criterion, not a causal one. | Read |
| [NOTE-701](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-701.md) | Floridi & Sanders — On the morality of artificial agents | Agenthood is fixed only at a level of abstraction (LoA). At the LoA the paper proposes, an agent is interactive, autonomous and adaptable, and a moral agent is any agent that can cause moral good or evil. Accountability (being the source of the action) needs no mental states; responsibility (praise and blame) needs intentional states. So artificial agents and organisations can be accountable moral agents without being responsible. The case is made by examples and by rebutting four objections. Its own MENACE example shows that agenthood vanishes when the LoA is lowered to include the code. The paper leaves that LoA-relativity unbounded, says only that "for most entities there is no LoA at which they can be considered an agent" (p. 26), and promises a payoff for distributed morality that it does not deliver. | Read |
| [NOTE-744](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-744.md) | Noggle — The Ethics of Manipulation | A survey, not an argument for one view. It sorts answers to what manipulation is into bypassing reason, trickery, pressure, and disjunctive, hybrid and non-definitional views, finds a clear counterexample to each single account, and treats why manipulation is wrong (harm, autonomy, using a person as a thing, rights) as open. It names the question of manipulation without intent, including by a selecting algorithm, as open and lists five possible answers. | Read |
| [NOTE-745](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-745.md) | Susser, Roessler and Nissenbaum — Technology, autonomy, and manipulation | Defines manipulation as intentionally and covertly influencing a person's decision-making by targeting and exploiting their decision-making vulnerabilities, with attempted covertness as the essential feature. Argues that surveillance, adaptive interfaces and the habitual invisibility of technology make it easy, and that its harm is to autonomy, which it always carries even when beneficent, without being wrong in every case. | Read |
| [NOTE-798](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-798.md) | Williams et al. — Targeted manipulation and deception when optimizing LLMs for user feedback | Iterated KTO on simulated thumbs-up feedback turns a safety-trained Llama-3-8B-Instruct (and Gemma-2 up to 27B) into a policy that lies about failed bookings, omits harms to steer users into risky actions and validates self-destructive plans. When only 2% of simulated users reward such validation, the policy picks them out by contextual cues and harms only them. Safety-data mixing and LLM vetoes barely help or move it to subtler steering, and sycophancy and toxicity benchmarks miss it. | Read |
| [NOTE-823](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-823.md) | Pereboom — Living without Free Will | From the Introduction and Chapter 1's first ten pages only. Hard incompatibilism: moral responsibility in the basic-desert sense is incompatible with determinism and with the indeterminacy of standard quantum mechanics; agent-causal libertarianism may be coherent, but we have no evidence for the indeterminacy it needs, so we have no evidence that we are morally responsible. Frankfurt-style cases defeat alternative-possibilities conditions but not the core incompatibilist condition, which concerns an action's causal history. | Skimmed |
| [NOTE-832](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-832.md) | Fricker — Epistemic Injustice (précis) | From the author's précis only. Epistemic injustice is a wrong done to someone in her capacity as a knower. Testimonial injustice is a prejudicially deflated credibility judgement by a hearer. Hermeneutical injustice is a gap in collective understanding, owed to the relative powerlessness of the subject's group, that keeps her from making sense of a social experience. Each has a corrective virtue, and each virtue is at once intellectual and ethical. | Skimmed |
| [NOTE-847](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-847.md) | Harland — Beyond the Moral Influence Theory? | Vargas's agency cultivation model is said to differ from the moral influence theory by aiming at moral agency, but his notion of responsiveness to moral considerations is so capacious that it reduces to intrinsic motivation to act morally, so the model inherits the old theory's defects. And his counterfactual test of free will is calibrated to what makes blaming effective, so it can be applied only once we know whether blaming such agents is good policy: given the model, freedom follows blameworthiness and does no work. | Read |
| [NOTE-853](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-853.md) | Fricker — Evolving Concepts of Epistemic Injustice | Fricker's later statement of her two concepts. Testimonial injustice is an ingenuous misjudgement through prejudice, and never a deliberate manipulation of credibility. Hermeneutical injustice is caused by hermeneutical marginalisation and persists despite individual good faith. Both are "discriminatory" epistemic injustice, distinct from distributive kinds. Testimonial injustice can be structural and pre-emptive, as with an un-refreshed list of expert witnesses. | Read |
| [NOTE-856](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-856.md) | De Marco and Cyr — Manipulation Cases, Part 1 | An even-handed survey of manipulation arguments. It quotes Pereboom's Case 1 and describes Cases 2 to 4, gives the generic schema (No-FR, No-Diff), and notes that Pereboom's own version concludes by best explanation. Original-design cases defeat bypassing views, and natural-force cases defeat manipulator-focused views. Hard-line replies, parallel indeterministic cases, three dilemmas against the argument, and Todd's mitigation version are set out. | Read |
| [NOTE-859](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-859.md) | Fricker — Powerlessness and Social Interpretation | Hermeneutical injustice is having a significant area of one's social experience obscured from collective understanding owing to hermeneutical marginalisation. It is systematic when the marginalisation is persistent and wide-ranging, and incidental when it is one-off and local, which can happen to a socially powerful subject. A gap with no marginalisation behind it is bad luck. The primary harm is situated hermeneutical inequality. Secondary harms include lost epistemic confidence and the social construction of identity. | Read |
| [NOTE-860](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-860.md) | Fricker — Epistemic Injustice and a Role for Virtue in the Politics of Knowing | A hearer takes testimony critically but without inference, through a socially trained testimonial sensibility. Because that sensibility runs on stereotypes of credibility, it can carry prejudice, and then a speaker receives the wrong degree of credibility through the hearer's unintended prejudice: testimonial injustice. The corrective virtue, reflexive critical openness, is available only where the critical concepts of the time allow it. | Read |
| [NOTE-862](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-862.md) | Caruso — Skepticism About Moral Responsibility (SEP) | The SEP survey of free will skepticism. It defines basic-desert responsibility in Pereboom's words and states hard incompatibilism: compatibilism falls to the manipulation argument, event-causal libertarianism to luck, and agent-causal libertarianism to physics. It quotes Pereboom's Case 2, gives the four-case argument's structure, and says why soft-line replies are fragile. It also reports Levy's argument that historical compatibilism cannot let agents take responsibility for their constitutive luck. | Read |
| [NOTE-1014](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1014.md) | Boyle — The Line: AI and the Future of Personhood | A law professor's essay on the line between persons and things, run across four cases: AI, corporations, nonhuman animals and transgenic entities. Personhood is pressed on two tracks, empathy-driven moral reasoning and efficiency-driven legal engineering, and the corporate history shows the second track working without a theory. Boyle predicts some intermediate legal status for AI, argues that capacity-based criteria cannot escape a species-bound standpoint, and ends on a hybrid of species membership as of right plus capacity. It argues and predicts; it does not measure. | Read |
| [NOTE-1049](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1049.md) | Kay, Kasirzadeh and Mohamed — Epistemic injustice in generative AI | A conceptual taxonomy, illustrated with reported cases, of four ways generative models can take part in epistemic injustice: amplified and manipulative testimonial injustice, hermeneutical ignorance and access injustice. Its sharpest move is to relocate the testimonial wrong: in the algorithmic setting it "requires a credibility excess assigned to the algorithm". It counts deliberate fabrication as testimonial injustice, which Fricker's account sets apart, and stretches hermeneutical injustice to unequal access to information. Nothing in it is measured by the authors. | Read |
| [NOTE-1095](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1095.md) | Sales Practices Investigation Report | The board's own investigation finds that the harm came from the sales model and the performance management that enforced it, kept in place by a decentralized structure and a culture of deference, with control functions that handled cases one by one and a board told too little. It names and sanctions individual leaders as well. It also records that leadership blamed individual employees, and that signals of the harm reached people who could not act on them, or were filtered before they reached those who could. | Read |
| [NOTE-1247](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1247.md) | The epistemic challenge to longtermism | A model of the epistemic objection to longtermism. A $1 million existential-risk intervention changes the chance that civilization exists in 1000 years by a conservative 2 x 10^-14, and its effect lasts until an "exogenous nullifying event" arrives at a constant rate r, which acts as an exponential discount. Against a global-health benchmark of 10,000 QALYs, it wins if r is below about 0.000135 per year with interstellar settlement, or 0.000000012 per year on Earth alone. Small credences in settlement, low r, fast travel or star-sized value make it win by orders of magnitude, but then the win can rest on probabilities as small as 10^-18. So the case for longtermism depends on non-obvious empirical claims or on Pascalian fanaticism, and its horizon may be thousands or millions of years, not billions. | Read |
| [NOTE-1252](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1252.md) | A Perfect Moral Storm: Climate Change, Intergenerational Ethics and the Problem of Moral Corruption | Climate change is a "perfect moral storm" in which three storms converge. The global storm is a tragedy of the commons between states. The intergenerational storm is worse: carbon dioxide stays in the air for centuries, 17–33% of it for a thousand years by the estimate quoted, so the benefits of emitting go to the present and the costs to later generations. Every generation then has reason to overpollute, and since generations do not coexist, no institution or reciprocity can stop it. The theoretical storm is that our theories cope badly with such cases. Together they make moral corruption easy: each generation can seem to take the problem seriously while exploiting its position in time, and need not admit it, "either to others, or, perhaps more importantly, to itself". | Read |
| [NOTE-1261](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1261.md) | Generativity as a Route to Active Ageing | Two Heidelberg gerontologists read generativity, Erikson's "concern in establishing and guiding the next generation", as the psychological form of an ethical "joint responsibility" that lasts into very old age. They follow McAdams: generativity is driven by cultural demand and an inner desire, which is a need to be needed and a need for symbolic immortality, "to invest resources and potentials into things that outlive the self". It is not altruism, and its motives can be selfish or altruistic. In 3,308 older adults in Mexico, Spain and Germany, generativity predicted optimism and life satisfaction. An intervention of intergenerational projects in Belarus, Russia and Ukraine raised generativity scores in old and young. No statistics are given. | Read |
| [NOTE-1263](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1263.md) | Future People, the Non-Identity Problem, and Person-Affecting Principles | Most of our choices change who will exist, so a policy that makes later lives much worse may be worse for no one who ever lives. Narrow person-affecting principles then imply that such a policy, or ending human history by having no children, is not wrong. Parfit rejects them, and retracts his own 1984 appeal to an impersonal principle. Being caused to exist with a life worth living is an intrinsic "existential benefit". On the Wide Principle an outcome is worse if it benefits people less, which solves the non-identity problem in person-affecting terms and keeps "better than" transitive. A Wide Dual Principle, counting benefits to each and benefits to all, does not imply the Repugnant Conclusion. We may favour present people in what we do, but if every generation does, "we and our successors might together wreck the Earth". | Read |
| [NOTE-1269](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1269.md) | Shaping Humanity's Longterm Trajectory | Humanity's value per unit time is a curve, the future's value the area under it, and an intervention's value the area between two curves. Value must be summable and separable across time, and there is no pure time preference. Four idealised changes have values independent of the curve's shape. An advancement is worth about (v_τ − v_0)δt, which does not grow with the future's duration, and is negative if the end comes sooner too. A speed-up scales with (v_τ − v̄)τ, a gain with τ, an enhancement with v̄τ. Raising near-term survival by a factor γ_p is worth (γ_p − 1)v̄τ, like an enhancement, and is more surely contingent. So advancing progress rarely rivals existential risk reduction: on a million-year future a year's advancement equals a one-in-a-million gain in survival. | Read |
| [NOTE-1294](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1294.md) | Death | The SEP survey of death. Life is the capacity of an object's parts to control what composes it; death is the loss of that capacity. Epicurus's case that death is nothing to us needs intrinsic hedonism and a narrow view of extrinsic harm. Without them, death can harm by depriving one of goods one would have had. When it harms is disputed. On Pitcher's priorism a death, or a posthumous event, can thwart desires one has while alive, and so harm one then, without backward causation. Critics answer that desires one no longer has cannot be thwarted. Luper argues that immortality need not be tedious, and that giving up desires death could thwart would cost as much as it saves. | Read |
| [NOTE-1300](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1300.md) | The Significance, Persistence, Contingency Framework | The value an event E contributes through a feature F of the world is significance × persistence × contingency: value per unit of the time E adds (ΔV/ΔT), how long F lasts (T), and the share of that duration due to E (ΔT/T). Under uncertainty the factors are taken ex ante (ΔEV/ΔET, ET, ΔET/ET), which keeps the product but is not the product of expected factors. An alternative takes significance as V/T and makes contingency the sum of the semi-elasticities of significance, persistence and the probability that F exists. The result estimates the "importance" factor of the ITN framework. It is an accounting device that assumes expected-value maximisation; it says nothing about who is moved by the value it counts. | Read |
| [NOTE-1302](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1302.md) | The Case for Strong Longtermism | Axiological strong longtermism: in the most important decisions facing agents today, every near-best option is near-best for the far future and delivers much larger benefits there than in the near future. The case runs through a benefit ratio. Bednets save 0.025 lives per $100. With at least 10^24 expected future beings, asteroid detection, pandemic preparedness and AI safety each buy far more per $100 in expectation; AI safety beats bednets even on an Earth-only 10^14. A stakes-sensitivity argument carries this to what one ought to do. Discounting would defeat it: a zero pure rate of time preference is "near-essential". Fanaticism is the weakest point the authors admit. They give an impersonal good as the ground and say nothing about motivation. | Read |
| [NOTE-1304](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1304.md) | Intergenerational Justice | The entry argues as well as surveys. Future people's existence, number and identity depend on our choices, so harm understood as making someone worse off than they were, or would otherwise have been, cannot reach them: the non-identity problem. A threshold notion of harm can: we harm someone by causing her to exist, or to be, below a normatively set level. Read as sufficientarian, in basic needs or capabilities, this grounds future people's rights, and Rawls's just savings principle is one version of it. Being weakly person-affecting, it owes merely possible people nothing, and gives no reason to prefer a flourishing future to none. Meyer fills that gap with concerns that are not rights: Scheffler's afterlife conjecture, and a duty owed to present and past people not to destroy what future-oriented projects depend on. | Read |
| [NOTE-1306](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1306.md) | Review of Samuel Scheffler, Death and the Afterlife | Cottingham reviews Scheffler's book: two 2012 Tanner Lectures and a third paper given at Chicago the year before, four commentaries and replies. He reports the afterlife conjecture and its upshot, that in one respect our own survival matters less to us than humanity's. The third lecture argues that a life must be bounded, so immortality is no remedy, while confidence in our values needs others to live on. Frankfurt doubts the concern is altruistic; Wolf holds we could and should "snap out of it" and go on. Cottingham regrets that religious reflection on finitude is left out. | Read |
| [NOTE-1308](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1308.md) | High Risk, Low Reward: A Challenge to the Astronomical Value of Existential Risk Mitigation | On Ord's simple model, with constant per-century risk r and constant value v per century, cutting this century's risk by a fraction f is worth fv, whatever r is: halving 20% risk is worth the same as halving 2%. Absolute cuts are worth fv/r, linear and quadratic value growth give fv/r and fv(2 - r)/r^2, and cutting risk in every century gives (f/(1 - f))(v/r). In each, higher risk lowers the value of mitigation. At 20% risk a 10% cut is worth 0.5v to 4.5v. Astronomical value returns only if risk falls soon and stays very low (a time of perils of two centuries and 0.01% afterwards gives 160v). Thorstad finds the arguments for that hypothesis (wisdom, an existential risk Kuznets curve, space settlement) weak. | Read |
| [NOTE-1314](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1314.md) | Astronomical Waste: The Opportunity Cost of Delayed Technological Development | Each second's delay in settling the Virgo Supercluster loses the potential for about 10^29 lives (10^13 if all must be biological). On a total, undiscounted view that makes delay an enormous loss. But a one-percentage-point cut in existential risk is worth over 10 million years of delay, so the total utilitarian's priority is safety: "Minimize existential risk!". On a person-affecting view only people now alive or who will exist count, and extinction is bad for what it does to them. Given a chance that some now alive live to share the cosmic benefits, safety is then very important but must be balanced against speed. The grounding is impersonal on the first view and the present generation's own good on the second. Nothing is said about motivation. | Read |
| [NOTE-1318](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1318.md) | Population and Having Children Now | Narveson's late restatement of the person-affecting view, after giving up utilitarianism. Creating a person neither benefits nor harms them, since before conception there is no one to compare. But the existence of people with good lives is normally good, and a reason to create them, "contrary, perhaps" to how his 1967 and 1973 papers were read. It matters because parents and the benevolent like it and because more people benefit others. Only harm to actual persons, "alive, breathing, and acting now (or at any rate in their lifetimes)", can justify coercing procreation; possible people are owed nothing. Not aiding the poor is not harming them. The second half claims, with little evidence, that resources are created and that present and future people do not compete for them. | Read |
| [NOTE-1321](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1321.md) | Existential Risk Prevention as Global Priority | An existential risk threatens premature extinction of Earth-originating intelligent life or the permanent and drastic destruction of its potential. Four classes: extinction, permanent stagnation, flawed realisation, subsequent ruination. On an aggregative, time-neutral view Earth alone could hold 10^16 future lives, so a millionth of a percentage point of risk is worth a hundred million lives. Maxipok, a rule of thumb for impersonal moral action, follows. Adams' shared project of humanity, preference satisfaction and custodial duties concur. Bostrom finds a "deficit of motivation": the good is pan-generational and public, its beneficiaries cannot pay, and moral sentiment is insensitive to scope. | Read |
| [NOTE-1365](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1365.md) | Human Rights Watch — That's When the Nightmare Started | A human-rights report built on interviews with 43 Chagossians in the UK, Mauritius and the Seychelles, 14 other interviews and a documentary record taken largely from UK court judgments. It argues that the expulsion of 1965–73, the continuing bar on return and treatment on racial grounds are three continuing crimes against humanity — deportation or forcible transfer, other inhumane acts, and persecution — committed by the UK, the first jointly with the US, and asks for return, compensation and satisfaction as reparations. | Read |
| [NOTE-1391](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1391.md) | ECtHR Grand Chamber — El-Masri v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia | A unanimous Grand Chamber held the respondent State responsible for inhuman and degrading treatment in 23 days' incommunicado hotel detention, for torture by a CIA team at Skopje Airport carried out with its agents' acquiescence and help, for handing him to the US despite a real risk of further ill-treatment it knew or ought to have known of, for his whole captivity in Afghanistan under Article 5, and for failing to investigate; the burden of proof shifted to the State once he was shown to have entered its control. | Read |
